The Wrinkled hornbill (Rhabdotorrhinus corrugatus), a large-bodied bucerotid from the lowland forests of Southeast Asia, exhibits a suite of life-history traits that reflect its reliance on seasonal fruit abundance. During incubation, which proceeds at an average temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the embryonated egg requires approximately 29 days [ab = approximately 29 days] to complete development and hatch. This incubation period is relatively extended for a bird of its body size, likely reflecting the energetic constraints of the altricial nestling that emerges. The newly hatched chick emerges weighing roughly 30 grams [Wwb = roughly 30 grams], a modest mass that quickly escalates under intensive parental provisioning. This wet weight at birth represents a small fraction of the adult mass, indicating a substantial growth trajectory ahead for the nestling.

As the nestling develops within the sealed tree cavity, it undergoes a rapid phase of mass increase. The provisioning adult birds, often assisted by auxiliary group members typical of many hornbill species, deliver a steady supply of figs and other drupes to the confined chick. Under the warm thermal conditions of the nest, which typically hover around 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the developing bird reaches the critical fledging milestone at approximately 70 days after hatching [tx = approximately 70 days after hatching]. This age at fledging, spanning roughly 65 to 73 days, represents the point at which the flight feathers have fully matured and the young bird is capable of sustained flight. Upon leaving the cavity, the fledgling remains dependent on adults for several more weeks as it refines its foraging skills.

Following fledging, the juvenile enters a protracted period of growth toward its ultimate adult dimensions. Full adult body mass, or ultimate wet weight, in this species reaches approximately 1590 grams [Wwi = approximately 1590 grams] for mature individuals. This large size, combined with a bill and casque adapted for fruit handling, positions the species as a crucial seed disperser within its ecosystem. The attainment of sexual maturity, marking the onset of gonadal activity and the ability to reproduce, occurs relatively late compared to smaller-bodied passerines. Puberty is achieved at approximately 210 days after hatching [tp = approximately 210 days after hatching] under the typical ambient temperatures of 40 °C [T = 40 °C] that characterize its tropical lowland habitat, underscoring the slow pace of life history common among large frugivorous birds.

The reproductive schedule of the Wrinkled hornbill is constrained by the availability of nesting cavities and the energetic demands of chick-rearing. Females typically produce clutches containing two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], a modest number consistent with the K-selected strategy of large tropical birds. Furthermore, reproductive events are not annual; instead, females will generally lay only one clutch each two years [F_R_i = annual; instead, females will generally lay only one clutch each two years], reflecting the high investment per offspring and the time required for the female to recover condition after her period of confinement within the sealed nest. This low maximum reproductive rate, combined with the long developmental period, results in a slow population turnover. The time since birth at first brood, or the initiation of a female's first successful nesting attempt, is typically deferred until approximately 3 years since birth [tR = approximately 3 years since birth], a delay that allows for complete somatic growth and mate acquisition at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C].

Longevity records for this species under natural conditions indicate a remarkable lifespan for a tropical bird of its size. Data from mark-recapture studies and observational records suggest that individuals can live for up to 50 years [am = up to 50 years] in the wild when maintained at ambient temperatures around 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This extreme lifespan, rivaling that of some parrots and albatrosses, is a classic correlate of a slow life-history pace characterized by low annual fecundity and late reproductive maturity. The combination of a 50-year maximum lifespan, a long juvenile phase, and a low annual reproductive output of only two eggs per clutch every two years places the Wrinkled hornbill firmly among the most slow-living of the Asian bucerotids. Such demographic parameters make the species particularly vulnerable to habitat loss and fragmentation, as population recovery from any decline is necessarily a multi-generational process.
